uses: Turmeric's bright orange rhizome has a long place in Ayurvedic, Chinese, Islamic and Thai medicine, where it was traditionally given for stomach and skin complaints, colds and stiff joints. In Europe Culpeper gave it to clear a blocked liver or spleen and for jaundice, though by Grieve's time it was valued mostly as a coloring. The EMA recognizes it as a traditional remedy for a slow digestion, fullness and wind. In the kitchen it is the golden base of curry powders, and it has long served as a yellow dye.
taste: Bitterish and slightly sharp, warming like ginger
energetics: Culpeper called turmeric hot in the third degree
caution_pregnancy: Turmeric supplements may be unsafe during pregnancy, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal turmeric in pregnancy or breastfeeding because safety hasn't been established. Liver injury in pregnancy has been reported with high turmeric intake. Little is known about more than food amounts while nursing. Avoid medicinal amounts; ordinary cooking amounts aren't the concern.
caution_medications: Turmeric may increase the risk of bleeding with blood thinners and anti-platelet drugs such as warfarin; this comes from lab studies and a case report. High intake raised levels of the transplant drug tacrolimus and harmed one patient's kidneys. It may change how chemotherapy drugs and drugs broken down by liver CYP enzymes act, mostly shown in lab studies. Talk to your provider first if you take any medicine.
caution_conditions: Do not use it with a blocked bile duct, bile duct inflammation, gallstones, other gallbladder disease or liver disease, since it may stimulate bile. Liver damage has been reported with curcumin supplements, especially products made for better absorption; stop and see a provider if you notice tiredness, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine or yellow skin or eyes. If you are prone to kidney stones, ask a doctor first. Side effects can include nausea, reflux, stomach upset, diarrhea, constipation, dry mouth and rashes. Use isn't established for anyone under 18.
caution_duration: Ordinary turmeric products are likely safe for up to 2 or 3 months. If digestive symptoms last more than 2 weeks, or get worse, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Curcumin on the skin can cause hives, itching or allergic dermatitis. Turmeric also stains skin, cloth and counters a deep yellow.
garden_harvest_timing: Dig the rhizomes in late fall or early winter, once the leaves die back and the plant goes dormant.
garden_water: Rich soil with plenty of organic matter
notes: A ginger-family perennial from southern Asia, about three feet tall with broad leaves and pale yellow-white flowers. Plant pieces of fresh rhizome, each with a bud, in early spring, letting cut pieces dry for a few days first to prevent rot. It dies back in winter cold and returns in late spring in warm climates. The leaves can be used to wrap food. Turmeric paper, soaked in the tincture, was once used by chemists as a test paper. Culpeper gives it no planet.
